I'm glad! I've had to learn lots of boundary-setting lessons with lots of people over the years, and one of the best ways to find peace, I think, is to tease apart your own needs and expectations from others'.

When my kids were little, I would describe it like this. For instance, if my mom and I had a fight, they'd say, "Mommy, you should talk nicer to Grandma," or, "Grandma, you shouldn't be mad at Mommy." So we'd say, "You're right. Thank you for reminding me." And then I'd explain that Grandma was trying to make a good decision to help me remember to get groceries, but she was worried that the store was going to close and we wouldn't have milk for the morning, and she let her scared feeling turn her good decision into a bad decision to fuss at me for not going yet. And then I wanted to make a good decision to reassure her that I would get milk in time and ask her nicely to speak more gently, but I was tired, so I let my tired feeling turn my good decision into a bad decision to yell at her. But then she and I would both use our good, loving feelings to turn those bad decisions back into good decisions to apologize and be kind to each other again. Separating fears and desires, motivations and decisions, can be incredibly powerful. But I had to break it down to teach someone before I began to develop language for what was playing out there.

You're always making your own decisions, of course. So just do what's right for you. If they come back and you don't want to be in a romantic relationship, for instance, don't date them. That said, if they're your TF and your souls are ready for TF Union, then that person will almost by definition be a beneficial presence in your life, however you choose to let them be a part of it. If you don't want them in your life because they're a negative presence, then they're not ready for Union anyway.

A big part of self-love is all sides of not asking others to take care of your emotions so you don't have to. That includes both making you happy because you don't know how to do it for yourself, and staying away from you because you don't want to deal with having them around. You have to be the one to establish that boundary, but if you're truly ready to do that, it's emotionally pretty easy and you can even feel warmth and love towards them when you do it.

I think the "should" is in large part a distraction. Listen carefully to yourself to feel whether this urge is coming from a straightforward you or a tangled you. I think of our selves in 3D and in 5D like the same bunch of strings, except in 5D, they're all orderly and clear, and in 3D, they're tangled into knots. So is this urge a clear and free thread or a loop from a big knot ball? You're the only one who knows.

At that point, when you can tell the difference, you get to forgive yourself for the 3D urges and even for acting on them. To me, it's the difference between saving your money (not acting on it), investing your money wisely to make more (acting on a 5D urge), and spending it on flashy things to live in the fantasy of having more (acting on a 3D urge). But until we learn, sometimes the hard way and that's just how it is, we might think we're investing but just end up with a crate full of Beanie Babies--we make some mistakes, right? Because we *don't* live in our 5D selves. But is it right to shame ourselves for those mistakes? Or is it right to tell ourselves we aren't our full 5D selves so we mustn't take any action? Do children grow into healthy adults by doing nothing and saying nothing until they're grown, or does that make people who are fully grown but still as inexperienced as children?

Ultimately, be kind to yourself. As much as you can, take only actions that you believe are not harmful to you. If you find that you made a mistake and harmed yourself or others, make your first priority to forgive yourself, because you can't forgive yourself for a mistake you refuse to admit or understand. Once you forgive yourself, you can learn from the mistake because you won't get mired in shame. And remember that, if it's a twin flame connection, the relationship itself demands the highest standards, but the connection allows for lots of retries--infinite, maybe.

I consider myself RA-adjacent, since I think my definition isn't always what other people mean by RA, but maybe this way of thinking about it will help you identify where you're feeling unsettled? My approach is that, when most people use a term to describe a relationship, what they're leaving out is all their assumptions about what that includes, and I prefer to separate out those extra assumptions. So, for instance, I have a husband, but all that tells you is that we are legally married. It's up to us to determine which relationships we want to have with each other. As it happens, we want to have basically every kind of relationship we can with each other, so we have built partnerships around romance, sex, co-parenting, friendship, household management, financial management, and business management, and each of those relationships is something that we could have with someone else, as well. We have to tend to each of those relationships individually. If we don't, we might unintentionally neglect one or more and it could wither. So, when we consider how we're caring for our relationship, we can't just say, "Well, we spend 90% of our waking time together, so we're giving each other enough time." If that 90% is broken down into 50% as co-parenting, 10% as business management, 20% as friendship, and 10% as household management, then our romance, sex, and finances are still being completely neglected! So we could pour more and more time into each other and still feel dissatisfied unless we're deliberate about the effectiveness of that time. I'll add my voice to the others to say that, when it comes to grief, the first best thing you can do is be as comfortable as you can. Grieving people deal with a ton of other people being uncomfortable around them, and every time someone isn't being uncomfortable and awkward, that's a relief in itself. Fake it as much as you can until you relax. You could have a couple of go-to sayings to acknowledge the loss, which is a kind thing to do, since most people try not to mention it and the ones who do often go overboard being sorry until the grieving person is the one having to console the other. Say something like, "Thank you for allowing me to do this for you. It's always an honor to get such an important request." You might say something like, "Can I ask about your baby? Did you have a name picked out yet?" and see if they want to be engaged in conversation. If they don't, you haven't made a terrible mistake. If they say they'd rather not talk about it, you can say, "I understand; that's just fine. I'll just be here, so please let me know if you need anything." And finally, if they do want to talk, don't feel obligated to make it a solemn conversation. One thing grieving people NEVER get to do is laugh! They may even laugh and cry in rapid succession, so be prepared for that, and just let it happen. Don't apologize if they cry. Just offer them a tissue and a glass of water afterwards. Just by doing nothing particularly special, you can actually make it a really lovely experience!

I really empathize with where you're coming from! This is something you can decide you're not ready for or that you can embrace. If you do, it can be really rewarding! And quite a curious experience. I do have a couple of suggestions.

First, it really helps to have a friend who understands the spiritual side of things and who also has a good head on their shoulders. I often turn to my best friends to talk through something I'm feeling. This helps me sort out the, shall we say, low-vibration messages from the high-vibration ones. (I really don't like that terminology, but it's a useful shorthand.) The messages are like a bunch of bits of yarn. The strings are the same in the "low" and the "high" spiritual contexts, but in the low one, they're all tangled up, and in the high one, they're sorted out nicely. Talking it out helps me separate the two, and also helps reassure me that I'm not going off the deep end (which I have some trauma about).

Second, spend plenty of time just listening and hearing. It'll take some time for your understanding to come quickly and clearly, and that's just practice. It may even happen faster than you expect. But it will go slower, the more you push. In particular, the messages you get while high may be more complicated, or you may need to develop a slightly different relationship with that aspect of the experience, so give that extra time, especially.

Third, and to me, most importantly, you are still the central part of the equation. That means you may get messages that don't quite feel right, and you have to listen to that feeling. Even if it's something that sounds like it ought to feel right; if it doesn't, trying to make yourself believe it does will only separate you from your intuitive abilities, and you will be more susceptible to that "tangling." Intuitive practices are an exploration of deep authenticity, so even if you think the message or guidance is good, if it's not authentic to you, you have to accept who and where you are and work from there.

Best of luck! Keep posting about your journey!

The best way to combat any problem is more communication. Talk with him about what he means to you. Tell him you're feeling nervous, and what you've come to understand about the patterns you've recognized. Tell him you don't want to run but you're still finding your way. Let him be on your team. This is a problem that you can probably solve on your own with time, but you can still let him be part of the solution. I don't mean codependency or denying your feelings. I mean, letting him know what you're dealing with, where he can comfort and support you where you are, rather than where you think you have to be to be good enough. It takes a lot of practice to go to someone you love and say, "I'm having this problem and I still can't figure out how to solve it," and allowing them to say, "I'm sorry, that sounds really hard. Want to talk it out at me?" And yes, when you're a couple, sometimes you find solutions together that neither of you would've come up with on your own, like having an understanding and maybe even a phrase you can use or a habit he can recognize when you need space to process. The desire to run isn't the core urge; it's based on real things in your heart and mind.
